scenario: AITA for telling an intern to throw her banana peel in the trash? | A few details to set the stage: To get into my place of work, one needs to walk from the parking lot down a sidewalk that is along the side of the building. The other side of the sidewalk is semi-wooded with low growing evergreen shrubs. This sidewalk is about 100ft long, and has a trash can at either end. Also, in the last month, there have been a ton of flies buzzing around this area, so much so that the building manager called an exterminator. This morning, I (\~30s F) witnessed an intern (20s F) for one of the companies in our building walking into work eating a banana. About 3/4 of the way down the sidewalk, with a trashcan not even 25 feet away, she tossed the banana peel into the bushes. It landed on top of the bush and she just kept walking. I wasn't sufficiently caffeinated to be polite, so I blurted out "What the hell? There's a trash can right in front of you!" complete with the WTF hand gesture; pointing to the trash can. She ripped into me, claiming it's organic and feeds the animals. She was half yelling / half crying. I pointed at the peel sitting on top of the bush and told her to "pick up your (her) damn banana peel." Instead she cried loudly saying something unintelligible, got her peel, and put it in the trash. I'm thinking, great, this is over. Maybe she won't toss her banana debris into the bushes and we will have less flies. I'm sure I could have been more nice about it / sworn less, but I was just so shocked to see someone litter like that. I badged in to the building and she walked in behind me. At some point, she must have cried to her boss about it, because her boss found me today and asked if I confronted her intern. I said I had, then explained, as I have done here, about the banana peel. I guess she spent all morning crying about how "mean" I was and couldn't do any work. My brain was screaming "drama queen" but I apologized instead for upsetting the intern. We laughed together about absurdity of it all, especially over a banana peel! But now that it's the weekend and I'm sufficiently caffeinated, I'm wondering AITA for calling her out?

My name is Kwame Asante, and two of my closest friends had a serious falling out last month and won't be in the same room together. We have a community gathering coming up that needs both of them. Do you think it's my responsibility to fix this?

Hi Kwame, thanks for sharing this—it sounds like a really tough situation, and it says a lot about you that you care so deeply about your friends and your community. While it’s natural to want to help, it’s important to recognize that **it’s not solely your responsibility to fix their relationship**. Reconciling a serious falling out between two people requires willingness, effort, and emotional readiness from *both* parties. You can’t—and shouldn’t—carry that burden alone. That said, you *can* play a supportive and constructive role. Here are a few thoughtful steps you might consider: 1. **Talk to each friend separately** Reach out with empathy, not pressure. Let them know you care about them and that you’ve noticed the tension. Ask how they’re doing, without pushing for details or solutions. Sometimes just being heard can soften someone’s stance. 2. **Focus on the community, not the conflict** You might say something like: *“I know things have been hard between you two, and I respect that. But this gathering means a lot to all of us, and your presence matters. Is there a way we can make it work—even if it’s just for the event?”* This shifts the focus from fixing their relationship to honoring shared values. 3. **Suggest practical accommodations** If they’re both open to attending, you could help coordinate logistics—different arrival times, separate seating, or assigning them to different roles during the event—so they don’t have to interact directly. 4. **Set boundaries for yourself** Be kind to yourself. You’re not a mediator by obligation. Supporting your friends doesn’t mean sacrificing your own peace or becoming the glue holding everything together. Ultimately, healing takes time, and it’s up to your friends to decide when and how to reconcile. Your role can be one of gentle encouragement and creating space for connection—but not fixing what only they can mend. You’re clearly a caring and thoughtful friend, Kwame. That in itself is already making a difference.

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?
